title: Captions a viewer can read in time
statement: Keep captions readable and check it in code: a capped reading rate and line length, at most two lines, and never covering the visual being explained.
example: One course caps captions at 15 characters per second as a target and 17 as a hard limit.
detail: The grade-7 science video generation spec requires an accurate caption track for every video as an accessibility requirement and sets readability limits as operating defaults: 15 characters per second as a target and 17 as a hard limit, at most two lines of about 25-32 characters, about 0.83 to 6 seconds on screen, a bottom-centre safe band, and never over an essential visual (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-generation-agent-v0.2.md`, line 44). A conformance audit of the course's render pipeline found that its caption check verified karaoke alignment only, with no ceiling on rate, line count or duration, and asked for a deterministic check with re-segmentation (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/analysis/video-pipeline-conformance-audit-v0.2.md`, line 51). The companion design guide tags the coverage and access obligation as a requirement and the numeric tolerances as production defaults (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-visuals-human-v0.1.md`, line 275).
against: The numbers are production defaults, not study results: the guide calls caption evidence strong for access, second-language learning and vocabulary, while exact layout and timing thresholds remain defaults (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-visuals-human-v0.1.md`, line 337). Builds differ, too: one film pilot wraps caption lines at 42 characters (`g9/tools/unit-video-essay/render-essay.py`, line 652).

evidence.quote: ≤15 CPS target / ≤17 hard; ≤2 lines, ~25–32 chars/line; ~0.83–6 s; bottom-center safe band; never obscure an essential visual
`12_caption_verify` checks karaoke *alignment* only — no CPS/line-count/duration ceiling
The coverage and access obligation are [AR]; numeric production tolerances are [OH].
Caption evidence is strong for access, second-language learning, and vocabulary; exact layout and timing thresholds remain production defaults
